label: Murchison Letter Never Published
detail: The forged-bait letter from a British minister, seen as favoring the President, never appears in the press, so the diplomatic row and the Irish-American backlash do not arise.
assumption: Without the letter and the dismissal of the British minister, Irish-American and anti-British sentiment is not inflamed late in the campaign, so Irish-born and Irish-descended voters in northeastern states behave as they did before October, a small shift back toward the party of the administration.
facts_text: No letter from the British minister at Washington on the coming election has been printed in the newspapers.
The British minister remains at his post and relations between the two governments are quiet, with no controversy over foreign interference in the contest.
research_questions: How did Irish-American voters in New York and other northeastern states shift between early October and election day 1888 after the letter was published?
How much did the dismissal of the British minister change the Irish-American vote compared with earlier tariff-centered campaigning?
Did voters in places with few Irish-born residents react to the letter in any measurable way?
source_text: The Murchison letter, in which the British minister appeared to favor Cleveland, is never published in October 1888.
